title: KMP algorithm: Knuth-Morris-Pratt string search in Python — cv.cm
description: KMP string search explained: the prefix function (failure table), a traced example, Python code that finds every match in O(n + m) time, and common mistakes.
h1: KMP string search explained: how it works, code and complexity
answer: The Knuth-Morris-Pratt (KMP) algorithm finds every occurrence of a pattern of length m in a text of length n in O(n + m) time. It first builds a prefix function (also called the failure table) for the pattern: for each position, the length of the longest proper prefix that is also a suffix. When a mismatch happens, KMP uses this table to shift the pattern without ever moving backward in the text.

body: String search asks where a short pattern occurs in a longer text. The naive method tries every start position and compares characters one by one. On ordinary text it is fast, but on repetitive inputs it is slow: searching for `aaaab` in `aaaaaaaaaa` compares almost the whole pattern at each position, which gives O(n × m) time.
KMP never re-reads a text character after a mismatch. Donald Knuth, James H. Morris and Vaughan Pratt published it in 1977 in "Fast Pattern Matching in Strings".

Suppose you are searching for the pattern `ABABC`, you have matched `ABAB`, and the next text character is not C. The part you just matched, `ABAB`, ends with `AB`, which is also how the pattern begins. So you already know the next attempt starts with 2 matched characters, and you can continue comparing from pattern position 2 instead of starting over.
The prefix function stores these numbers. `pi[i]` is the length of the longest proper prefix of `pattern[0..i]` that is also a suffix of it (proper means not the whole string).
For example, `pi[4] = 3` because `ABABA` begins and ends with `ABA`. `pi[5] = 0` because no prefix of `ABABAC` ends with C.
Search for the pattern `ABABC` (prefix function 0, 0, 1, 2, 0) in the text `ABABABC`. The variable k counts how many pattern characters are currently matched.

body: The naive algorithm is O(n × m) in the worst case but often close to O(n) on natural-language text, so KMP's advantage shows mainly on repetitive data.

ul: Off-by-one in fallback: after a mismatch, set `k = pi[k - 1]`, not `pi[k]`. `pi` is indexed by the last matched position.
Using `if` instead of `while` for the fallback: you may need several fallbacks in a row before a character matches.
Forgetting to reset k after a full match: set `k = pi[k - 1]` to find overlapping matches, or `k = 0` for non-overlapping ones.
Concatenation trick: compute the prefix function of `pattern + separator + text`, using a separator that appears in neither; every position where the value equals m is a match end.
The Z-algorithm computes a closely related array and also searches in O(n + m).

body.note: In everyday Python code, use the built-in `str.find`, the `in` operator or `str.count`. They are implemented in C and are much faster than a pure-Python KMP. Write KMP when you need it for an interview, for a custom alphabet (lists of tokens, not strings), or when you need the prefix function itself.

ul: Interview problems: implement `strStr()`, shortest palindrome (prefix function of `s + "#" + reversed(s)`), repeated substring pattern, smallest period of a string (`m - pi[m - 1]`).
Real world: searching in DNA sequences and network packet streams, where linear worst-case time matters.

faq.q: What is the prefix function or failure table in KMP?
faq.a: For each position i of the pattern, it stores the length of the longest proper prefix of `pattern[0..i]` that is also a suffix of it. On a mismatch, KMP uses it to know how many characters are still matched.

faq.q: What is the time complexity of KMP?
faq.a: O(n + m): O(m) to build the prefix function and O(n) to scan the text. It is linear even in the worst case.

faq.q: Is KMP faster than Python's str.find?
faq.a: No. `str.find` is implemented in C with an optimized search algorithm and is much faster in practice. KMP is valuable for its guaranteed linear time, for learning, and for non-string sequences.
Yes, if after a full match you set `k = pi[k - 1]` instead of 0. For example, it finds `AA` at positions 0, 1, 2 and 3 in `AAAAA`.
